Dissent

/dih-SENT/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Dissent means to disagree, especially with an official decision or widely held position.

When the board approved the merger, one director chose to dissent, warning that the deal would double the company's debt overnight.

Worked Example

When the national gardening society officially endorsed a new pesticide, Dr. Reyes chose to dissent, publishing an open letter questioning the chemical's safety record. Her dissent prompted the society to order an independent review.

Dr. Reyes did not just privately disagree; she pushed back against the society's official position, which is exactly what dissent describes. The second sentence shows the noun form of the word: her dissent is the expression of that disagreement itself.

How Dissent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disagree

disagree: to hold a different opinion

oppose

oppose: to argue or act against something

differ

differ: to hold another view

Antonyms

assent

assent: to agree formally

concur

concur: to share the same opinion

How Strong Is It? — disagree → dissent → defy

disagree vs. dissent

disagree vs. dissent: Disagree is the everyday, milder word; you can disagree about where to eat lunch without taking any formal stand.

defy vs. dissent

defy vs. dissent: Dissent is stronger than disagree because it pushes back against an official position, but defy goes even further, openly refusing to follow the decision at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: apart, in a different direction

Root — sent

Root — sent: to feel or think (Latin sentire)

Put it together

Put it together: Dissent is built from dis- (apart) plus sent (to feel or think), so it literally means to feel or think apart from others. When you dissent, your thinking splits away from the official view.

Use the root in a new word: sentiment

Use the root in a new word: sentiment: The mayor's speech perfectly captured the public sentiment about the new park.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / civic

Common collocations: dissent from a ruling, a dissenting opinion, voices of dissent. As a noun, dissent names the disagreement itself. Compare objection: an objection is one specific, often formal statement of opposition, while dissent is broader, ongoing disagreement with an official position.
